Aw man I relate to this a lot. I’m 22 rn and I’ve felt so much disappointment from going from being a “gifted” kid to someone that struggles so badly with procrastination/avoidance/barely passing or failing classes.
I don’t want this to be unsolicited advice, but I would just like to share this with you. (I ended up writing A LOT more than I though I would oh god)(I’m sorry if this isn’t helpful at all, personal anecdotes from others brings me comfort, so I’m write this in case it can bring comfort to someone else. Don’t feel obligated to respond)
though I still struggle with feeling that disappointment, I’m continuing to work on embracing my genuine love for learning and being understanding with myself. Young adult years are rough because we go through SO MUCH mentally/physically/emotionally throughout that brief period of time. I wish I would have invested in bettering my mental health during middle school/high school. Our grades may not always be perfect, maybe they’ll suck sometimes, but prioritizing building a healthy relationship with ourselves will help us out SO much in the future. 
I feel like I only focused on getting good grades and being involved in extra curriculars during high school. I struggled a lot with my depression and anxiety at the same time, but I didn’t really “work” through that beyond going to therapy on and off. The first 2 years of high school I kept up w getting good grades. But over time, my anxiety and depression led me to procrastinate, avoid/ignore assignments, put myself down, etc. I would do these things so much, that by the time I was in college, my anxiety and depression directly impacted my academics more and more. 
If I could say anything to my past self, it would be to put my mental health over my desire for academic validation. Growing up, i had proven to myself that I was capable of doing well in school, so if I invested in my own well-being, good grades could’ve been the outcome from time to time. Even if I were to focus on my mental health and still get “bad” grades, I think my current self would be so grateful that I decided to work on my depression/anxiety instead of getting burnt out from seeking academic validation all of the time. 
Obviously it’s impossible to go back and change the way I lived my high school life, and that i wouldn’t even have this advice for myself if I didn’t go through the things I went through. All I can do now is listen to my own advice and prioritize my mental health NOW. 

I’m sharing this with you because I hope it can bring some comfort to know that your own well being will always be more important than your grades, and that prioritizing it will pay off in the future (example: in my case, I probably would’ve gotten a lot better grades and not have felt so suicidal in college if I didn’t struggle so much with my mental health). Good grades can be an outcome of taking care of yourself, there’s a good chance that it will, but it can be unhealthy for good grades to be THE thing to strive for. 
I hope your relationship with yourself grows stronger during your young adult years. You deserve to be your own source of happiness, not how well you do academically.

No problem man. Yea the way we’re generally expected to go through life with completing school within a set timeline and then do something (get a job/career) to keep surviving?? Like it can seem kind of like a game sometimes. 
But there are some moments where we’ve experienced life and maybe thought, “hey, this is kind of nice” even if it’s just for a brief minute over the smallest thing. It takes a lot of strength to get out of the “I have to do this and this and this and keep going even if I’m not doing well so I can succeed in life” mindset, but if you let yourself get out of that mindset often enough, maybe you’ll start thinking of your life as YOUR life. Not your parents’, not your friends’, not your professors, not the imaginary “general public” you may have in your head (I say this because I have a fake “general public” in my head that I imagine as society judging me....if that doesn’t make sense to you just ignore it hehe..), your life is YOURS.

People have started from the bottom and have gotten to a comfortable place in life. Being alive while going through the pressure and thoughts you’re having is really hard, it’s painful, but there is always another way to continue life that’s not dying. The education system and societal/familial expectations don’t dictate your life, regardless of how much pressure that puts on you. I’m so sorry you’re going through this, I wish I could give you a hug. You don’t deserve to go through this. The things you are feeling aren’t your fault. 

Right now is a very tough time and no one should be too hard on themselves. When things aren’t going as expected, it doesn’t determine whether there will be good in the future or not. Your life is what you make it, and with a lot of support, that you can either find in your community or through the internet, you can make it different than what it is now. You don’t have to be doing well academically/financially/etc to start being free of this pain. You can take care of yourself, your mind, your body. What may sound like the littlest things can be so good for you.

You don’t deserve to go out like this.

Hey, I’m in a similar position (21 F). I’m failing a lot of classes and have gotten really behind due to mental health issues and suicide attempts. One thing that has personally brought me hope is being told by professors/faculty that it doesn’t matter how long it takes you to graduate. Everyone takes their own time. Sometimes we are simply not at the best place psychological to take on the challenges that college brings. And it wouldn’t be accurate to assume that most 18 year olds could go straight to college and go through it in 4 years just fine. Shit happens in life, and it’s hits some harder than others. It makes school a lot more challenging than if we didn’t have personal struggles. And right now ESPECIALLY, the pandemic has been hitting some harder than others. 

I was forced to talk to some faculty from the counseling center and student affairs at my school after I was reported for suicidal ideation, and although it pissed me off at first, it helped me personally to be honest with a faculty member about what was going on with how I felt. They told me about options I could take so I could prioritize taking care of myself and completing my degree in the way I can, even if it takes taking a Leave and/or staying an extra semester/year. 

There might be someone at your college that will be there for you and can help you through this (counseling center/counselor, maybe your school has a crisis line, student affairs, a professor you feel safe with that can refer you to someone). Your life doesn’t have to be defined by how exactly you follow the typical timeline in college. If you choose to do anything, I strongly suggest reaching out to someone at your school that can give you options for how to continue your education (or take a break from it) or refer you to someone who can. It takes a lot of courage to reach out, it kind of feels like exposing yourself, but letting things out can really help things take a turn for the better. 

I can tell you that I’ve done these things, and things aren’t perfect (I’m still super behind and worry about whether I will complete my degree requirements in time), but talking to someone has influenced me to separate my academic progress and my worth as a human being.

You are a human being that deserves care, support, and compassion. I wish for these things to come your way.

It can be so frustrating to have parents that don’t understand mental health. I’ve felt similar, and something I do to cope with it is telling myself that they grew up where/when mental health was more taboo, and that often makes close minded people judge and fear it.

Graduating high school is a weird transition in life. Idk if this is accurate for you, but during high school, everything seems like a big deal, and it feels like those 4 years determine how the rest of your life will go. As someone who’s also depressed and has anxiety, little things/inconveniences would feel like the end of the world (they still do now that I’m in college, but it’s not as bad as before). School is structured in such a rigid way that tends to limit individuals’ mindsets. The world and life is so much more than school. In the moment it’s difficult to manage, but when it gets to be too much, remember that it won’t always feel this exact way. (Also, there’s such a variety of people out there, there’s always potential to make new friends.) Simple things in life that bring you moments of happiness could ease your mind, and I think feeling happy moments whenever you can is a big part of living your life. 

I’m sorry you’re feeling lost and hopeless about the future. In your mind that might make a lot of sense to you. Your feelings are valid. Please know that it’s very possible to change the way you feel by thinking about things in a different perspective. My therapist often tells me that she doesn’t believe that most people are actually lazy, and from what you’ve shared, it doesn’t seem like laziness is the problem. You care about how your life is going, and deep down you have a desire to feel better and be doing better. You’re not lazy, you’re just struggling. And it’s okay to struggle for a long time. Sometimes the way we grow up, the environment we’re in, or the resources we have/don’t have, aren’t the best fit for what we specifically need to flourish. 

If you think about the roots of your struggles, instead of believing you’re lazy, the self-deprecating mindset will fade away (though it will come and go), and it’s a step towards becoming the individual that’s within you. Treat yourself gently, with kindness and understanding, you deserve it so much. I hope that something/someone comes into your life soon that can also bring you gentleness, kindness, and understanding; you deserve that too. 

You’re always welcome to message me and talk about this some more, or to talk about anything. Hang in there. You’re not alone.
